newsitem.title: USA: IMF seeks bank, budget action in Thai reform plan.
newsitem.headline: IMF seeks bank, budget action in Thai reform plan.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund threw new light on its plans for the battered Thai economy on Tuesday, highlighting tough action to deal with ailing banks and curb the budget gap as government priorities.

IMF First Deputy Managing Director Stanley Fischer told CNN's Business Asia programme that the authorities had agreed to a tough set of measures as part of a package of economic reforms being drawn up with IMF help.
The interview, broadcast only in Asia, was made available to Reuters in Washington.

"The programme is not quite finalised -- they will continue negotiations on the plane on the way back from Tokyo to Bangkok -- but we want the exchange rate to float...and we want very rapid action on financial companies which are essentially insolvent," Fischer said.

"They have to be very resolute in dealing with banking sector problems and the budget has to come into stronger balance in order to make sure that the current account deficit can be financed. There is a pretty tough set of measures which the Thai authorities have agreed to do."
The economic reform programme now being negotiated will underpin a $16 billion rescue package for Thailand, including loans of $4 billion from the IMF and $4 billion from Japan.

Other countries in the region, announcing their intentions after a special donor meeting in Tokyo on Monday, have also promised to contribute. Even China -- joining an international aid package for the first time -- is likely to help.
"Regional powers were interested in cooperating with Thailand, they did not want to see a major economy in the area go any deeper into difficulty," Fischer said.
He added: "China has not yet committed how much it is going to offer to Thailand in this package but it has said it probably will.

"I am sure it wants to indicate that it can play a constructive role in the region, and this is an opportunity for it to help. It also probably worries about the possibility that there could an adverse affects on Hongkong if the Thai problem is not resolved promptly."

The Hongkong authorities said on Tuesday they spent US$1 billion in July defending the Hong Kong dollar against speculative attacks. The currency, managed under a currency board system which links cash in circulation to central bank reserves, has been pegged at 7.8 per U.S. dollar since 1983.

The Thai authorities reluctantly sought IMF help last month when it became clear they would need extra resources to close financial holes which emerged after they were forced to allow the baht currency to float.

The United States has not joined the package, but Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said on Monday the United States expected to back an IMF programme. Summers said he expected measures to improve the health and openness of the financial system to form a substantial part of the IMF plan.

Fischer, who said the United States was contributing to the Thai bailout in its role as the IMF's largest single shareholder, also said the fund would have welcomed contributions from outside the Southeast region.

He added: "We would have been happier if there had been more contributions from outside the region as well, but obviously the people the most involved are the neighbours and it is likely to go that way in future as well," he said.

The Thai loan was the biggest loan package for a single country since the United States led a $40 billion bailout for Mexico in early 1995. Mexico never took up all funds available and Fischer said this could be the case for Thailand too.
